SiteProof

A web application in which a small contractor keeps the complete record of each job in one place: photos and short videos taken into the job, markup, daily logs, checklists, change orders and completions signed on a phone, estimates, invoices and payments, private links and a portal for customers, and guest links for subcontractors. Originals are stored unchanged with a cryptographic fingerprint, customer views reveal only what the contractor selects, and three books set out the method for contractors.

A technician takes a photo with no signal. It waits in IndexedDB; when the network returns, the queue asks the server for a signed URL, uploads the file straight to storage, then calls complete. The server checks size and type by content, hashes it with SHA-256, derives a thumbnail and a display copy with sharp and inserts the row inside a transaction that runs as a restricted role with the user set, so row-level security decides what it may touch.

Key engineering decisions

01

Isolation in the database

Every request runs in a transaction under a role without bypass rights, with the user id set for that transaction; policies call helper functions for membership and write access. A forgotten WHERE clause in application code cannot leak another company’s rows.

02

Composite foreign keys on company

Tenant tables reference (id, company_id), so a photo can only point at a job of the same company. The schema refuses cross-tenant links even if a policy were wrong.

03

Uploads that bypass the server

Phones upload directly to storage through signed URLs and the server only finalises, which keeps large videos off serverless limits; originals are never modified.

Notes for reviewers

Data model57 tables in a siteproof schema: companies, memberships, jobs, photos, reports, estimates, invoices, signatures and an outbox. Public tokens for estimates, invoices and portals are stored only as SHA-256 hashes.
SecurityThe application role can read signatures but not change them; rate limits live in a table; customer links can expire, carry a password or be revoked; AI calls are capped at 300 per company per day.
TestingIntegration tests assert that one company cannot read another’s rows, that each demo is isolated and expires, and that storage limits hold. A production stall on a streaming read led to a 15-second read timeout.
Limits and next stepsConnect subscription billing and outgoing email, which are built but not switched on, and move thumbnail generation to a queue for very large batches.
01

Problem statement

For a small contractor, the record of a job is usually scattered across a camera roll, a text thread, a paper pad and the memory of whoever ran the work. Photos sent by text are compressed and lose their capture dates, changes are agreed by voice, and the person who took the pictures may leave the company with them. The cost appears later: a customer disputes a scratch that was already there, a change that was never written down, or an invoice for work that is now behind drywall; an adjuster asks for evidence; a buyer's inspector asks who installed the roof. Commercial products exist for jobsite photos, but the paperwork that turns a photo into proof, the signed change, the daily log, the estimate and the invoice, usually lives in other tools or nowhere.

02

Contribution

SiteProof treats the job as the unit of record and attaches everything to it. Capture is designed for the field: one camera button on every screen, labels Before, During and After, dictated captions, short videos, and an offline queue that uploads when the phone reconnects. Paperwork is built on the same record: sign-offs of five kinds store the exact statement with the typed name, the drawn signature, the time and the witness; estimates built from a price book are signed and accepted by the customer and become deposit or final invoices; payments are recorded against invoices whose status follows. Sharing follows an explicit privacy model: internal notes and chat are never exposed, and addresses and photo locations stay hidden on customer links unless a link is set to show them; a portal gathers everything shared with one customer, and guest links let subcontractors add attributed photos to one job without an account. Optional AI helpers suggest captions, read text in photos, draft checklists and daily logs, and translate messages, under the instruction never to invent work, dates, prices or causes. A per-visitor demo and three books, a field guide, a sales book and a book of 47 cases, present the method to contractors.

03

Architecture

The application is written in TypeScript with Next.js 16 and React 19 and runs on Vercel; mutations are server actions, and every sensitive action is authorized on the server, never by hiding a button. Data lives in a dedicated PostgreSQL schema on Supabase. Each request runs inside a transaction under a restricted database role with the signed-in user set for that transaction, and row-level security policies built on helper functions for membership, write access and ownership decide which rows are visible; tenant tables carry composite foreign keys on the record and its company, so a row can only point to rows of the same company. Trusted server tasks, such as public signing pages and the demo, use a separate system path. Files sit in a private bucket: the phone uploads directly through signed URLs, the server then checks size and type by content, computes a SHA-256 fingerprint and derives a 480-pixel thumbnail and a 2,048-pixel display copy with sharp, leaving the original untouched. Tokens for estimates, invoices, sign-offs, guest links and portals are stored only as SHA-256 hashes; customer links can expire, carry a password or be turned off. The application role may read signatures but not change them. Report PDFs are assembled with pdf-lib from stored data, the offline queue keeps photos and videos in IndexedDB, and dictation uses the browser's speech recognition. AI helpers call the Anthropic Messages API only when a key is configured, within 300 calls per company per day.

04

Method and data

Three rules governed the design. Nothing is invented: report fields left empty are omitted, every photo states where its capture time comes from (the camera's own record, the phone at the moment of capture, or the upload when neither exists), and AI prompts forbid unstated facts. Nothing is exposed by default: customer pages are built from an explicit selection, and location, captions, dates, markup and downloads are separate switches. Nothing is deleted by a limit: when storage is full, uploads are refused with a message and existing files stay; a lapsed account becomes read-only and exportable. Before & After reports pair photos by their labels and capture times. The demo is seeded from a shared template of photos and sample documents uploaded once at build time; each visitor receives new company rows that reference those files, creation is limited to 6 per network address per hour and 500 per day, and deletion code skips the template prefix so one visitor cannot remove files another sees. The books were written in Markdown, typeset with paged.js into 6 by 9 inch PDFs with the product's own screenshots, and every scenario in them is labeled as an invented composite, with no testimonials and no invented statistics.

05

Verification and limitations

Seventy-nine unit and integration tests run against PostgreSQL, among them tests that one company cannot read another's rows, that each demo is isolated and expires with its links, and that storage limits are enforced; six Playwright suites cover the main flows, and scripted browser runs exercised signing by link, accepting an estimate with a signature, invoicing a deposit and recording its payment, a guest upload and the portal. On production, creating a demo once stalled on a streaming read from storage; reads now time out after 15 seconds, and the demo no longer touches storage when it is created. A review of the sample data also found real place names left in early screenshots; the demo was moved to fictional places and the screenshots were retaken. Limitations: card billing for subscriptions and outgoing email are not yet connected, so invitation links are shared by hand; card payments from customers go through the contractor's own payment page; AI helpers require an API key; whether an electronic signature suffices for a given contract depends on the jurisdiction; SiteProof is not accounting or payroll software; and photos waiting offline exist only on the phone until they upload.
